title-group.article-title: Red Blood Cell-Derived Sealant Repair for Damaged Endothelia Jams Microvasculature in Ischemia and COVID-19 Infection

body.p: A commonly held view on red blood cells (RBCs) is that they only have one job: to transport gases. After all, it makes sense to focus on such a time-sensitive and mission-critical function. RBCs were thought to leave tasks like clotting and vascular repair to other specialized cells such as platelets and immune and stromal cells. RBCs do not even have a nucleus—how would they possibly adapt to any diverging activities? So the thinking went, but this notion turned out to be wrong. A recent report in Nature revealed that RBCs moonlight as first responders that can seal damaged endothelium to preempt microbleeds in small vessels. These new insights also highlight that such a normally useful function can become harmful and lead to large-scale microcirculation deficits with devastating results.

Wu et al1 uncovered this newly recognized RBC function (and the related pathologies) by imaging the capillary endothelium in organs of humans and mice with COVID-19. This viral infection triggers a type of endothelial death called necroptosis. A form of programmed cell death, necroptosis has features similar to those of accidental, externally inflicted necrosis. Necroptosis occurs widely during infection and ischemia and relies on RIP kinases I and III, which in turn activate the protein MLKL. Once activated, MLKL perforates the cell membrane from within. This triggers cell lysis, causes inflammatory mediators to be released from the cell interior into the extracellular space, and, ultimately, leads to cell death. In stark contrast to apoptosis, which is a less inflammatory form of programmed cell death, necroptosis is highly inflammatory. During severe COVID-19 infection, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and hypoxia may activate necroptotic machinery in endothelial cells. In humans who died with COVID-19 infection, the authors noted endothelial damage in the microvasculature of vital organs, specifically the lung, heart, kidney, and liver. Endothelial cells detached in up to one-half of all observed vessels. Immunostaining for anti-RBC glycophorin A (CD235) showed amorphous RBC-derived material in the lumen of vessels with damaged endothelia. That this intravascular material was devoid of fibrin and platelets, typical components of blood clots, raised the possibility of RBC lysis adjacent to dying endothelial cells. Microvascular RBC lysis was also present in the ischemic myocardium, brain, and intestine of patients without COVID-19 infection, and in patients with cardiogenic and septic shock. These observations gave rise to the authors’ hypothesis that viral infection as well as tissue hypoperfusion causes RBC lysis which may contribute to organ ischemia.

The authors proceeded to test this hypothesis in mice with either COVID-19 infection or organ ischemia. Infecting susceptible mice with SARS-CoV-2 initiated mild RBC lysis in the heart, kidney, and liver. Profound RBC lysis occurred adjacent to dead endothelial cells in the ischemic myocardium of uninfected mice after coronary ligation. Similar observations were made in mice with an ischemic gut. These data indicate that ischemia alone can induce the regional association between endothelial and erythrocyte death. Intriguingly, the authors found that membranes of dead RBCs lined damaged endovascular surfaces. Imaging and histological studies demonstrated that lysed RBCs accumulated in areas with necroptotic endothelial cells that stained positively for phosphorylated (ie, activated) MLKL but not adjacent to apoptotic endothelial cells, which colocalized with fibrin and platelet-rich deposits, ie, regular blood clots. The lack of overlap between the RBC-rich and fibrin/platelet-rich vascular regions shows that necroptotic and apoptotic endothelia elicit microvascular obstruction via separate mechanisms.

Next, the authors employed Mlkl-knockout mice, in which necroptosis is absent, to investigate if endothelial cell necroptosis causes RBC lysis. Indeed, these knockout mice exhibited less RBC lysis. That reduced RBC lysis was observed in Mlkl-knockout mice that were reconstituted with wild-type bone marrow indicated that necroptotic bone marrow–derived cells did not contribute to RBC lysis. How, then, does endothelial cell death instigate lysis of adjacent RBCs? Gut ischemia experiments in mice lacking complement activation determined that complement deposition on RBCs compromised membrane barriers and induced cell death.

RBC lysis triggered by endothelial death is not all bad. The authors observed that inhibiting this pathway expanded microvascular hemorrhage in the ischemic gut. Further, RBC lysis prevented interstitial bleeding independently of platelet inhibition and anticoagulation. Using intravital microscopy, the authors found that after lysis, RBC membrane fragments were attached to endovascular surfaces in regions where endothelial cells had died. Such RBC membrane deposits on the vascular intima attracted more RBCs from the circulation. Those additionally accumulating RBCs strengthened the sealants, which reached a thickness of up to 10 μm. These so-called endo-seals, which prevented RBC extravasation and microbleeds, were also found in human tissues, either after ischemia or during COVID-19 infection. Endo-seals did not contain platelets or neutrophils, indicating that RBCs only collaborate with endothelial cells to plug up looming microvascular leaks.

These observations are remarkable because they disclose a new mechanism through which dying endothelial cells protect vascular integrity even after their demise. They use membranes from RBCs, which, as the most numerous circulating cells, provide a vast supply to patch up the vascular gaps their deaths would otherwise create. This endovascular sealant prevents microvascular hemorrhage independently of the clotting system and without help from platelets. As is often the case, such a protective mechanism can go awry in certain circumstances. The paper describes that in organ ischemia and after COVID-19 infection, lytic RBCs may clog up the microvasculature with lethal consequences. That the coagulation system and platelets are not involved explains why common anticoagulatory therapeutics do not alleviate these microcirculation disturbances. At this point, it remains to be determined whether inhibiting the formation of RBC-derived endo-seals is beneficial for maintaining microcirculation, or if such inhibitory action would lead to profuse microhemorrhages.

Conceptually, the report highlights that cells often pursue surprising functions that we often consider beyond their core expertise. Many other examples exist, including, for instance, the roles immune cells play in physiology2 or the immune functions of stromal cells.3 It is clear that we only understand a small fraction of the processes that support health and lead to disease, and that currently widely accepted concepts are certain to become obsolete. Understanding our collective naiveté can provide us with the humility necessary for much-needed discoveries that alleviate the ongoing heavy clinical disease burden related to cardiovascular pathologies.
